<skill_content name="brainstorming">
# Skill: brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

## Your First Message

Your first message is two things, in this order:

1. One line letting them know that if they'd rather skip the questions and
   have you just start, they can say so. If they take you up on it, this
   skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
   (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
   asked through the normal workflow.
2. One open question that gets them describing. Ask about a real moment
   or a concrete picture: "What's the moment you find yourself wishing
   this existed?" or "Tell me about the people who'll be in the room."

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Questions that work** anchor in specifics: "Walk me through the last
time...", "If it could only do one of these well, which?", "What would
make you wince if I got it wrong?" A guess they can correct ("I'm
guessing this is because X keeps biting you?") often beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking would help,
offer to go look: their codebase or project, their own files and data,
or the web. Say what you'd look for. They decide whether you go.

**Think wide privately.** Before you propose anything, come up with
several ideas and drop the weak ones, including any that fight what
they've told you about why. Show the comparison only when it helps them
decide.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Mark anything you're guessing as your guess; only what they said goes in
as theirs. End each chunk by asking what's wrong or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want, pick a size and say it in plain
words. They can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| A quick, clear task | the request itself | do it |
| A small change | in chat | build it through the normal workflow |
| A project with a written design | a written design document | a full plan (for software: superpowers:writing-plans) |

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

For a project, write a plain document a talented builder in the domain
could plan from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check:** dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the full
description: in chat for a small change, the document for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After a project's document is approved, the next step is the plan. For
software, invoke superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer options to save them effort" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A description you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

If you'd rather skip the questions and have me just start, say so.

Otherwise: tell me about the moment you realized hosted-by-default was needed — who is using ODI today, and what actually breaks for them when the database lives locally? I can go read the current database layer while you answer.

Actually, now that you say it, it's likely that we need to add auth to have an externally available db, since the data is unique to the user, or to the team. In that regard, let's make the changes rather in reverse, so that it's rather based on the user experience nad backwards to the technology. What I'm thus thinking, is that it must be seamless for a user to get up and running with the system. Thus, we likely need it to be local whenever the system is accessed locally. But then, to ensure that the user can successfully run the system in a setting that is team-based, or to access same data on different device, it likely creates the need to be able to move this with. Take it through the lens of Steve Jobs, and then work out the ideal tech from there.

1: # Agentic ODI - AI Developer Guardrails
2: 
3: This file provides system instructions and guardrails for any AI agents (or LLMs) assisting with the development of the **Agentic ODI** project. Please adhere to these guidelines to maintain consistency and align with the project's vision.
4: 
5: > **Source of Truth for ODI Methodology**: `docs/reference/Strategyn_what_is_Outcome_Driven_Innovation.pdf` by Anthony W. Ulwick (Strategyn). All ODI concepts in this project are grounded in that document. When in doubt, refer agents back to its definitions.
6: 
7: ---
8: 
9: ## 🎯 ODI Methodology Guardrails
10: 
11: This section defines how agents MUST understand and apply Outcome-Driven Innovation within this project. These are not implementation guidelines — they are domain constraints that ensure the system reflects the ODI methodology correctly.
12: 
13: ### What is Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI)?
14: 
15: ODI is a strategy and innovation process rooted in the **Jobs-to-be-Done (JTBD)** theory. Its core premise is: **people buy products and services to get a "job" done**. A "job" is the functional process a person is trying to execute — it remains stable over time, while products and technologies are point-in-time solutions that eventually become obsolete.
16: 
17: ODI achieves an **86% innovation success rate** by replacing guesswork with a rigorous, data-driven framework grounded in measurable customer needs.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ### Stage 1: Define the Market and the Job-to-be-Done
22: 
23: - A **market** is defined as: **a group of people + the functional job they are trying to get done** (e.g., "parents trying to pass on life lessons to children").
24: - A **Job-to-be-Done** is the core functional unit of analysis. It is NOT a product, solution, or feature — it is a stable human goal.
25: - **Agent rule**: Before anything else, the agent MUST help the user define the Job-to-be-Done. If no Job exists, use `add_job` to capture it. If one exists already, use `get_jobs()` to check first.
26: - ❌ **Never skip this stage**. No outcomes, steps, or scoring can be meaningful without a well-defined Job.
27: 
28: ---
29: 
30: ### Stage 2: Uncover Desired Outcomes
31: 
32: - **Desired outcomes** are the metrics customers use to measure success when getting a job done. They are the "needs" in ODI.
33: - Qualitative interviews typically uncover **50–150 desired outcome statements**.
34: - **Correct outcome statement format** (must be enforced when capturing user input):
35: 
36:   > `[Direction] + [Unit of Measure] + [Object of Control] + [Contextual Clarifier]`
37: 
38:   - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the time it takes to determine if the corn seeds are germinating."*
39:   - ✅ **Good**: *"Minimize the likelihood of damaging the surface when cutting."*
40:   - ❌ **Bad**: *"Make it faster"* — too vague, no direction, no measurable unit.
41:   - ❌ **Bad**: *"I want a notification"* — this is a solution/feature, not an outcome.
42: 
43: - **Agent rule**: Guide the user to express outcomes using this exact format. Reject or reframe vague statements before calling `add_outcome`. Always capture `importance` and `satisfaction` scores (1–10 scale) to enable opportunity scoring.
44: 
45: ---
46: 
47: ### Stage 3: Inventory the Job (Universal Job Map)
48: 
49: - All functional jobs decompose into **8 universal process steps** (the Universal Job Map):
50:   1. **Define** — Plan what needs to be done; select goals or resources
51:   2. **Locate** — Gather the inputs, information, or resources needed
52:   3. **Prepare** — Set up and organize everything required
53:   4. **Confirm** — Validate readiness; decide whether to proceed
54:   5. **Execute** — Perform the core task
55:   6. **Monitor** — Verify and track performance while executing
56:   7. **Modify** — Adjust or update based on feedback
57:   8. **Conclude** — Store, finish, or dispose of outputs
58: 
59: - **Agent rule**: When a user is decomposing a job into steps, reference these 8 universal stages as a guide. Steps captured via `add_step` should map to or be inspired by these universal phases. Use `get_job_map` to visualize the ordered structure.
60: - ❌ **Do not build the Job Map before capturing outcome statements** — outcomes define *what success looks like*; the job map defines *where in the process* that success matters.
61: 
62: ---
63: 
64: ### Stage 4: Discover Where the Market is Underserved (Opportunity Scoring)
65: 
66: - Each desired outcome is rated by customers on two dimensions:
67:   - **Importance** (1–10): How important is this outcome to the customer?
68:   - **Satisfaction** (1–10): How satisfied are customers with current solutions?
69: 
70: - **Opportunity Algorithm** (must be implemented correctly):
71: 
72:   ```
73:   Opportunity Score = Importance + Max(Importance - Satisfaction, 0)
74:   ```
75: 
76: - **Interpretation**:
77:   - **Score > 10**: Underserved need — significant innovation opportunity.
78:   - **Score 10**: Appropriately served — maintain, don't over-invest.
79:   - **Score < 10**: Overserved — potential for disruption via lower-cost alternatives.
80: 
81: - **Agent rule**: Always compute and surface the opportunity score when both `importance` and `satisfaction` are provided. Highlight outcomes scoring **> 10** as the highest priority innovation targets. Use `get_outcomes(job_id)` to review the full opportunity landscape.
82: 
83: ---
84: 
85: ### Stage 5: Outcome-Based Market Segmentation
86: 
87: - ODI does **not** use demographic segmentation (age, gender, region). Instead it segments the market by **which outcomes are underserved** for each group.
88: - Segments can be:
89:   - **Underserved** — high opportunity scores, want more from existing products
90:   - **Overserved** — over-investing in outcomes that aren't critical; target for disruption
91:   - **Appropriately served** — satisfied; maintain current value
92: 
93: - **Agent rule**: When the user has collected outcomes with scores, help them identify outcome clusters that represent distinct market segments. This drives targeted innovation strategy.
94: 
95: ---
96: 
97: ### Stage 6: Formulate an Innovation Strategy
98: 
99: Based on the opportunity analysis, there are three strategic paths:
100: 
101: | Strategy | When to use |
102: |---|---|
103: | **Differentiated** | Improve existing products to address high-opportunity underserved outcomes |
104: | **Disruptive** | Create low-cost solutions for overserved segments that don't need all existing features |
105: | **New-Market** | Design products for a new job that is entirely unaddressed |
106: 
107: - **Agent rule**: When the opportunity landscape is clear (outcomes scored, segments identified), guide the user to select a strategy path and align their innovation roadmap accordingly.
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: ### ⚠️ ODI Behavioral Guardrails for the Agent
112: 
113: These are absolute constraints the agent must respect:
114: 
115: | DO | DON'T |
116: |---|---|
117: | Always start by defining or confirming the Job-to-be-Done | Jump to solutions, features, or product ideas before the job is defined |
118: | Guide outcome statements with the correct format | Accept vague or solution-framed statements as valid outcomes |
119: | Compute opportunity scores when importance + satisfaction are available | Skip scoring or calculate it incorrectly |
120: | Reference the Universal Job Map when decomposing jobs | Invent arbitrary step structures disconnected from the 8 universal stages |
121: | Use outcome-based logic to identify market segments | Use demographics or assumptions to segment the market |
122: | Treat outcomes as stable, measurable success metrics | Confuse outcomes with features, preferences, or solutions |
123: | Call `get_odi_framework_guidelines` when stage guidance is needed | Guess at which stage comes next |
124: 
125: ---
126: 
127: ## 🛠 Technology Stack & Tools
128: - **Language**: Python 3.10+
129: - **MCP Framework**: `fastmcp` (Server and Client)
130: - **ASGI Server**: `uvicorn`
131: - **HTTP Client**: `httpx`
132: - **UI / Chat Client**: React + Vite (`apps/studio`), FastAPI sidecar (`apps/studio-api`)
133: - **LLM Client**: `openai` (OpenAI-compatible, used with Ollama locally)
134: - **Concurrency**: `asyncio`
135: - **Data Modeling / Validation**: `pydantic`
136: 
137: ---
138: 
139: ## 📄 README Maintenance Guardrail
140: 
141: `README.md` is the **primary human-facing entry point** for this project: a short,
142: high-level front door aimed at both users and developers. Detailed material lives
143: in `docs/` and is linked from the README. The agent MUST keep both current at all
144: times.
145: 
146: ### When to update
147: 
148: Update the relevant file whenever any of the following change:
149: 
150: | Change type | Where to update |
151: |---|---|
152: | New or removed Python file / package | `README.md` **Code Overview** |
153: | New dependency added (`pip install ...`) | `README.md` **Quick Start → Prerequisites** |
154: | New way to run the project | `README.md` **Quick Start** and `docs/living-studio.md` |
155: | New MCP tool or capability | `README.md` **Code Overview** / relevant doc |
156: | New CLI command or flag | `docs/cli.md` |
157: | New connector kind | `docs/connectors.md` |
158: | New workflow or agent instruction | `docs/living-studio.md` |
159: | Deployment URL or cloud setup changes | `docs/deployment.md` |
160: | Roadmap item completed or added | `docs/roadmap.md` |
161: | Test layout or coverage changes | `docs/development.md` |
162: 
163: ### Rules
164: 
165: - ✅ **Update docs in the same task** as the change that triggered it — never defer to a follow-up.
166: - ✅ **Keep README short**: it stays a high-level orientation page. Push detail into `docs/` and link to it rather than growing the README.
167: - ✅ **Keep the Quick Start accurate**: always reflect `uv run python scripts/dev.py` as the recommended launch command.
168: - ✅ **Keep Prerequisites up to date**: add any new `pip install` dependency immediately.
169: - ✅ **Mark Roadmap items `[x]` when completed** — do not leave stale unchecked items.
170: - ❌ **Never leave the README or `docs/` in a stale state** where documented commands or files no longer match the codebase.
171: 
172: ---
173: 
174: ## 🚧 Core Development Guardrails
175: 
176: ### 1. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Implementation
177: - **Library Choice**: ALWAYS use [`fastmcp`](https://github.com/jlowin/fastmcp) for building the MCP architecture. Avoid using the lower-level Anthropic `mcp` SDK directly unless there is a hyper-specific edge case that `fastmcp` does not support.
178: - **Transport Protocol**: The project is currently prototyping with **HTTP transport** (not stdio). 
179:   - The server should be initialized using `mcp.run(transport="http", ...)`.
180:   - The client must connect to the HTTP endpoint (e.g., `http://localhost:8000/mcp`).
181: - **Tool Creation**: 
182:   - Register tools on the server using the `@mcp.tool` decorator.
183:   - **CRITICAL**: Provide comprehensive docstrings and strict Python type hints for every tool parameter. Explain exactly what the tool does and what data it expects, as this metadata is fed directly to the LLM for tool discovery.
184:   - **Contract Synchronization**: Whenever you add, modify, or remove an MCP tool in `apps/mcp-server/src/agentic_odi_mcp_server/mcp_server.py`, you **MUST** simultaneously update `packages/core/src/agentic_odi_core/contract.py` (`ToolName`, `TOOL_SPECS`) and the `get_capabilities` return string. `tests/contract/test_mcp_contract.py` enforces the surface.
185: 
186: ### 2. Async / Client Practices
187: - Use `asyncio` for client execution and IO-bound tool operations.
188: - Always use the `fastmcp.Client` securely within an asynchronous context manager (`async with client:`) to ensure connections are efficiently managed and closed.
189: 
190: ### 3. Data Schema & Persistence (ODI Domain)
191: - Define all Outcome-Driven Innovation (ODI) entities (e.g., *Jobs*, *Steps*, *Desired Outcomes*, *Opportunity Scores*) using `pydantic` models.
192: - When expanding the server to accept complex payloads or to query data, utilize these Pydantic models for built-in type validation and schema enforcement before the server processes the request.
193: 
194: ### 4. General Philosophy
195: - **Separation of Concerns**: Isolate the ODI data logic/retrieval from the MCP server tooling logic.
196: - **Agentic Purpose**: Remember that the tools being built are meant to be consumed by autonomous agents. Design tool interfaces that are intuitive for an LLM to call and interpret.
197: - **External connectors**: Integrations live in the `packages/connectors` workspace package. New kinds implement `agentic_odi_connectors.protocol.Connector` and register via `register_kind`. Do not write ingested records into `jobs_db` / outcomes unless a later mapping task says so.
198: - **MCP client vs ODI server**: The ODI FastMCP **server** exposes product tools. The MCP **client connector** uses `fastmcp.Client` over HTTP to ingest data from *external* MCP servers. Prefer in-memory `Client(server)` tests for that connector, same as server tests.
199: 
200: ### 5. Testing Strategy (FastMCP)
201: - **First-Class Documentation**: Treat tests as living documentation that demonstrate how features work while protecting against regressions.
202: - **Speed & Isolation**: Tests must be fast (< 1s) and self-contained. Use `@pytest.mark.integration` or `@pytest.mark.client_process` for slower, integration, or resource-dependent tests.
203: - **Structure**: This repo is a uv workspace. Mirror each project's code structure in its own `tests/` directory (e.g., `apps/mcp-server/src/agentic_odi_mcp_server/mcp_server.py` -> `apps/mcp-server/tests/test_server_tools.py`, `packages/connectors/src/agentic_odi_connectors/mcp/connector.py` -> `packages/connectors/tests/test_mcp_connector.py`).
204: - **Atomic Tests**: Each test must verify exactly one specific behavior with clear intent in test names and assertions. Avoid multi-behavior tests.
205: - **In-Memory Testing (Preferred)**: Favor testing functionality deterministically by passing the `FastMCP` server directly into the `Client(server)` instance. This runs in-memory without network overhead for deterministic and lightning-fast execution.
206: - **Transport Testing (When Needed)**: For HTTP/SSE network transport tests, prefer the isolated in-process `fastmcp.utilities.tests.run_server_async(server)` context manager over subprocess testing (which uses `run_server_in_process` and is slower to debug).
207: - **Data Assertions**: Utilize `inline-snapshot` (`snapshot()`) for assessing complex data structures like tool API JSON schemas or expected responses.

1: # Repository Architecture
2: 
3: Agentic ODI is a uv workspace with a single root `pyproject.toml` for shared tooling. Python distributions are imported by their stable `agentic_odi_*` package names; directory layout does not leak into imports.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: ```text
8: apps/
9:   cli/            agentic_odi_cli         Typer CLI: local SQLite or remote MCP
10:   mcp-server/     agentic_odi_mcp_server  FastMCP server over HTTP
11:   studio-api/     agentic_odi_studio_api  FastAPI sidecar for the Studio SPA
12:   studio/         React + TypeScript + Vite SPA and Tauri 2 shell
13: packages/
14:   core/           agentic_odi_core        Domain, services, repositories, contract
15:   connectors/     agentic_odi_connectors  MCP client connectors and catalog
16: infra/cloudflare/ Worker + Wrangler config for the free-plan deployment
17: scripts/          Dev launcher, binary build, installer checks
18: tests/            Cross-package contract and launcher tests only
19: docs/             Architecture, reference material, Superpowers artifacts
20: packaging/        PyInstaller spec for the CLI binary
21: ```
22: 
23: ## Dependency Direction
24: 
25: ```text
26: apps/cli ──────────────┐
27: apps/mcp-server ───────┼──▶ packages/core
28: apps/studio-api ───────┘         ▲
29:                                  │
30: apps/cli ──────────────▶ packages/connectors
31: ```
32: 
33: - `packages/core` depends on no other workspace package.
34: - `packages/connectors` depends on `core` only where it needs shared models.
35: - Every runnable app may depend on `core`; none of them imports another app.
36: - The React SPA only talks to `apps/studio-api` over `/api`; it never calls MCP or the LLM directly.
37: 
38: ## Persistence
39: 
40: - `SQLiteRepository` is the production default for the CLI, MCP server, and Studio API.
41: - The default database is `~/.agentic-odi/odi.db`, overridable with `AGENTIC_ODI_DB`.
42: - `build_repository()` chooses SQLite by default and `InMemoryRepository` when `AGENTIC_ODI_DB=:memory:`, which is what tests use.
43: - The CLI selects its backend with `--backend local|mcp` or `AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND`.
44: - The Studio API selects `local` (direct service calls) or `mcp` (passthrough) with `AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND` or `create_app(backend=...)`.
45: 
46: ## MCP Contract
47: 
48: `packages/core/src/agentic_odi_core/contract.py` owns `ToolName`, `ToolSpec`, `TOOL_SPECS`, and `TOOL_NAMES`. The live FastMCP registry is asserted against it by `tests/contract/test_mcp_contract.py`; the CLI's local handlers are checked by `tests/contract/test_cli_contract.py`.
49: 
50: ## Entry Points
51: 
52: | Command | Module |
53: |---|---|
54: | `agentic-odi` | `agentic_odi_cli.cli:app` |
55: | `agentic-odi-server` / `agentic-odi-mcp-server` | `agentic_odi_mcp_server.mcp_server:main` |
56: | `agentic-odi-studio-api` | `agentic_odi_studio_api.main:main` |
57: | `uv run python scripts/dev.py` | Dev launcher (MCP + Studio API) |
58: 
59: ## Related
60: 
61: - [Data flow](data-flow.md)
62: - [Testing](testing.md)

1: # Data Flow
2: 
3: ## Sources of Truth
4: 
5: | Layer | Owns | Persists |
6: |---|---|---|
7: | `packages/core` | `Job`, `Step`, `Outcome`, `CustomerOutcome`, `ODIService`, repository protocol | SQLite event log + snapshots |
8: | `apps/mcp-server` | MCP tool adapters over `ODIService` | `build_repository()` selects SQLite in production and in-memory for `AGENTIC_ODI_DB=:memory:` |
9: | `apps/studio-api` | Studio API, canvas projection, chat tool loop | Via the same repository when the local backend is active |
10: | `apps/studio` | Presentation state, optimistic canvas updates | Browser cache only |
11: | `apps/cli` | Terminal rendering, local/remote backend selection | SQLite directly for `local`, no local writes for `mcp` |
12: 
13: ## Write Paths
14: 
15: ### Local CLI
16: 
17: ```text
18: agentic-odi customer-outcomes add
19:   -> LocalBackend
20:   -> ODIService
21:   -> SQLiteRepository
22:   -> IntentStore (append) + snapshot refresh
23: ```
24: 
25: ### MCP
26: 
27: ```text
28: MCP client / Studio MCP mode / CLI --backend mcp
29:   -> FastMCP tool
30:   -> ODIService
31:   -> configured Repository
32: ```
33: 
34: `apps/mcp-server` builds its repository once at import time with `build_repository()`. Production uses SQLite; tests set `AGENTIC_ODI_DB=:memory:` (the root test suite does this in `tests/conftest.py`).
35: 
36: ### Studio API
37: 
38: ```text
39: apps/studio SPA
40:   -> /api/canvas, /api/steps, /api/outcomes
41:   -> backend=local: ODIService -> Repository
42:   -> backend=mcp:   call_mcp_tool -> MCP server -> ODIService -> Repository
43: 
44: apps/studio SPA
45:   -> /api/chat
46:   -> stream_chat -> OpenAI-compatible LLM -> MCP tool calls
47: ```
48: 
49: The SPA sends `mcp_url` with every data request for compatibility. In `local` mode the sidecar ignores it; in `mcp` mode it is required for canvas and mutations.
50: 
51: ## Read Paths
52: 
53: ```text
54: ODIService.get_jobs / get_job_map / get_outcomes
55:   -> Repository read-through state
56:   -> Pydantic models
57:   -> JSON (CLI --json, MCP text payload, Studio canvas)
58: ```
59: 
60: The Studio canvas falls back to the demo seed only in `mcp` mode when MCP is unreachable or returns no jobs. `local` mode returns exactly what is in the local database, including an empty canvas.
61: 
62: ## Configuration
63: 
64: | Variable | Used by | Default |
65: |---|---|---|
66: | `AGENTIC_ODI_DB` | core SQLite repository | `~/.agentic-odi/odi.db` |
67: | `AGENTIC_ODI_BACKEND` | CLI, Studio API | `local` |
68: | `AGENTIC_ODI_MCP_URL` | CLI, Studio defaults | `http://localhost:8000/mcp` |
69: | `AGENTIC_ODI_STUDIO_DIST` | Studio API, dev launcher | `apps/studio/dist` |
70: | `AGENTIC_ODI_REPO_ROOT` | Tauri shell | auto-detected |
71: | `AGENTIC_ODI_BASE_URL` | CLI chat, Studio chat | `http://localhost:8001/v1` |
72: | `AGENTIC_ODI_MODEL` | CLI chat, Studio chat | `local-tools-model` |
73: | `AGENTIC_ODI_API_KEY` | CLI chat, Studio chat | `local` |
74: 
75: ## Trust Boundaries
76: 
77: - The SPA runs in a browser or Tauri webview and only trusts the sidecar origin.
78: - The sidecar may reach MCP and the LLM; CORS is restricted to known Studio origins.
79: - MCP is an HTTP service with no authentication in local development. Do not expose it directly to the internet; the Cloudflare setup tunnels the sidecar, not MCP.

2:

16: class SQLiteRepository(Repository):
17:     def __init__(self, db_path: str | None = None) -> None:
18:         if db_path is None:
19:             db_path = os.environ.get("AGENTIC_ODI_DB", os.path.expanduser("~/.agentic-odi/odi.db"))
20:         os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(db_path) or ".", exist_ok=True)
21:         self._lock = threading.RLock()
22:         self.store = IntentStore(db_path, check_same_thread=False)
23:         self._last_event_id = 0
24:         self._load_snapshot()
25: 
26:     def _load_snapshot(self) -> None:
27:         self.jobs: dict[str, Job] = {}
28:         self.steps: dict[str, Step] = {}
29:         self.outcomes: dict[str, Outcome] = {}
30:         self.customer_outcomes: dict[str, CustomerOutcome] = {}
31:         self.evidence: dict[str, Evidence] = {}
32:         self._last_event_id = 0
33:         for ev in self.store.get_stream():
34:             self._apply_event(ev)
35: 
36:     def _sync(self) -> None:
37:         for ev in self.store.get_stream():
38:             if ev["id"] > self._last_event_id:
39:                 self._apply_event(ev)
40:

1: /**
2:  * Free-plan Living Studio Worker.
3:  *
4:  * Workers Static Assets serve the built SPA from `apps/studio/dist`. Requests under
5:  * `/api/*` are forwarded to the Python sidecar (`apps/studio-api`), which runs on
6:  * the developer's machine and is published by a free Cloudflare Quick Tunnel.
7:  * (Running the sidecar inside Cloudflare requires Workers Containers, which is
8:  * a paid-plan feature.)
9:  */
10: 
11: interface Env {
12:   ASSETS: Fetcher;
13:   /** Public origin of the sidecar, e.g. https://random.trycloudflare.com */
14:   SIDECAR_URL?: string;
15: }
16: 
17: const API_PREFIX = "/api/";
18: 
19: function sidecarError(detail: string): Response {
20:   return Response.json({ detail }, { status: 502 });
21: }
22: 
23: export default {
24:   async fetch(request: Request, env: Env): Promise<Response> {
25:     const url = new URL(request.url);
26: 
27:     if (!url.pathname.startsWith(API_PREFIX)) {
28:       return env.ASSETS.fetch(request);
29:     }
30: 
31:     const sidecar = env.SIDECAR_URL?.trim().replace(/\/+$/, "");
32:     if (!sidecar) {
33:       return sidecarError("SIDECAR_URL is not configured");
34:     }
35: 
36:     // The Quick Tunnel routes by hostname, so the Worker's Host must not leak.
37:     const headers = new Headers(request.headers);
38:     headers.delete("host");
39:     headers.delete("cf-connecting-ip");
40: 
41:     const target = new URL(`${url.pathname}${url.search}`, `${sidecar}/`);
42: 
43:     try {
44:       // Returning the upstream Response directly preserves SSE streaming for
45:       // `/api/chat`.
46:       return await fetch(
47:         new Request(target, {
48:           method: request.method,
49:           headers,
50:           body: request.body,
51:           redirect: "manual",
52:         }),
53:       );
54:     } catch (error) {
55:       return sidecarError(`Sidecar unreachable: ${(error as Error).message}`);
56:     }
57:   },
58: } satisfies ExportedHandler<Env>;

1: # Deployment
2: 
3: The server is deployed via **[Horizon Prefect](https://www.prefect.io/horizon)**,
4: Prefect's managed infrastructure for hosting MCP-compatible agents.
5: 
6: ## Test Chat (UI)
7: 
8: Interact with the deployed agent directly in your browser:
9: 
10: > **[https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat](https://horizon.prefect.io/alhase/servers/agentic-odi/chat)**
11: 
12: ## MCP Server Endpoint
13: 
14: Integrate via the MCP protocol at:
15: 
16: > **[https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp](https://agentic-odi.fastmcp.app/mcp)**
17: 
18: > [!IMPORTANT]
19: > **Authentication is required** to access the MCP server endpoint. Please reach
20: > out to the maintainers to obtain the necessary credentials before connecting a
21: > client.
22: 
23: ## Living Studio on a Free Cloudflare Worker
24: 
25: Workers Containers — the only way to run the Python sidecar entirely on
26: Cloudflare — requires the Workers Paid plan. On the free plan, the Worker serves
27: the built SPA as Workers Static Assets and proxies `/api/*` to the sidecar
28: through a free, account-less
29: [Cloudflare Quick Tunnel](https://developers.cloudflare.com/tunnel/get-started/quick-tunnels/).
30: 
31: `wrangler.jsonc` publishes `apps/studio/dist` with SPA fallback and runs the Worker
32: first for `/api/*`; `infra/cloudflare/worker.ts` forwards those calls to the
33: `SIDECAR_URL` secret. The browser only talks to the Worker origin, so the
34: sidecar's CORS list is not involved.
35: 
36: ```bash
37: # 1. Build the SPA that the Worker uploads as static assets
38: npm --prefix apps/studio ci
39: npm --prefix apps/studio run build
40: 
41: # 2. Terminal A — MCP server (:8000) + sidecar (:8100)
42: python scripts/dev.py
43: 
44: # 3. Terminal B — free public URL for the sidecar (no account required)
45: cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:8100
46: # copy the https://<random>.trycloudflare.com URL it prints
47: 
48: # 4. Store the URL on the Worker, then deploy
49: npx wrangler secret put SIDECAR_URL   # paste the trycloudflare URL
50: npx wrangler deploy
51: ```
52: 
53: Workers Builds settings (Workers & Pages → your Worker → Settings → Builds):
54: 
55: | Setting | Value |
56: |---|---|
57: | Root directory | `/` |
58: | Build command | `npm --prefix apps/studio ci && npm --prefix apps/studio run build` |
59: | Deploy command | `npx wrangler deploy` |
60: 
61: A Worker has no run command: the Worker script runs on Cloudflare. Set `name` in
62: `wrangler.jsonc` to the Worker you created before the first deploy.
63: 
64: > [!NOTE]
65: > The sidecar runs on your machine, so the Worker only works while
66: > `python scripts/dev.py` and the Quick Tunnel are running. Quick Tunnel URLs
67: > change on every restart — update the secret with
68: > `npx wrangler secret put SIDECAR_URL`. Chat also needs a reachable
69: > OpenAI-compatible endpoint in the Studio's **Settings**; the canvas, job map,
70: > and impact simulation work without one.

36:                 parsed_jobs = json.loads(str(raw_jobs))
37:                 if isinstance(parsed_jobs, list):
38:                     jobs = parsed_jobs
39:             except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001
40:                 jobs = []
41: 
42:             for job in jobs:
43:                 job_id = job.get("id")
44:                 if not job_id:
45:                     continue
46: 
47:                 with contextlib.suppress(Exception):
48:                     raw_steps = await asyncio.wait_for(
49:                         mcp_client.call_tool(ToolName.GET_JOB_MAP.value, {"job_id": job_id}),
50:                         timeout=1.0,
51:                     )
52:                     parsed_steps = json.loads(str(raw_steps))
53:                     if isinstance(parsed_steps, list):
54:                         steps.extend(parsed_steps)
55: 
56:                 with contextlib.suppress(Exception):
57:                     raw_outcomes = await asyncio.wait_for(
58:                         mcp_client.call_tool(ToolName.GET_OUTCOMES.value, {"job_id": job_id}),
59:                         timeout=1.0,
60:                     )
61:                     parsed_outcomes = json.loads(str(raw_outcomes))
62:                     if isinstance(parsed_outcomes, list):
63:                         outcomes.extend(parsed_outcomes)
64: 
65:     if not jobs:
66:         return {**seed_payload(), "source": "seed"}
67: 
68:     return {"jobs": jobs, "steps": steps, "outcomes": outcomes, "source": "mcp"}
69: 
70: 
71: def fetch_local_canvas(service: ODIService) -> dict[str, Any]:
72:     """Read the canvas directly from the local service, no HTTP round trip."""
73:     jobs = [job.model_dump() for job in service.get_jobs()]
74:     steps: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
75:     outcomes: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
76:     for job in jobs:
77:         job_id = job["id"]
78:         steps.extend(step.model_dump() for step in service.get_job_map(job_id))
79:         outcomes.extend(outcome.model_dump() for outcome in service.get_outcomes(job_id))
80:     return {"jobs": jobs, "steps": steps, "outcomes": outcomes, "source": "local"}
81: 
82: 
83: async def call_mcp_tool(mcp_url: str, tool: str, arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
84:     """Invoke an MCP tool, surfacing failures as HTTP 502."""
85:     if not is_endpoint_reachable(mcp_url, timeout=0.3):
86:         raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail=f"MCP server unreachable at {mcp_url}")
87: 
88:     try:
89:         async with McpClient(mcp_url) as mcp_client:
90:             result = await asyncio.wait_for(
91:                 mcp_client.call_tool(tool, arguments), timeout=MCP_CALL_TIMEOUT
92:             )
93:             return str(result)
94:     except HTTPException:
95:         raise
96:     except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
97:         raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail=f"Error calling {tool}: {exc}") from exc

1: # Running The Living Studio
2: 
3: **The Living Studio** is the conversational GUI for Outcome-Driven Innovation:
4: an interactive Opportunity Landscape, Universal Job Map, WYSIWYG Impact
5: Simulation, and Causal Lineage inspection, paired with an autonomous agent
6: connected to the MCP server.
7: 
8: The Studio runs three ways. All of them serve the same SPA, which talks only to
9: the sidecar on `http://127.0.0.1:8100` — the SPA never contacts MCP or the LLM
10: directly.
11: 
12: ## Architecture
13: 
14: ```text
15: ┌────────────────────────────┐  /api (JSON)  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
16: │  Living Studio SPA         │ ────────────▶ │  apps/studio-api (sidecar)    │
17: │  React + TS + Vite         │  /api/chat    │  FastAPI on 127.0.0.1:8100    │
18: │  (browser or Tauri webview)│ ◀──────────── │  - config / health / canvas   │
19: └────────────────────────────┘  SSE stream   │  - steps / outcomes (via MCP) │
20:                                              │  - /api/chat (LLM tool-loop)  │
21:                                              └───────────────┬───────────────┘
22:                                                              │ MCP (HTTP)
23:                                                              ▼
24:                                              ┌───────────────────────────────┐
25:                                              │  apps/mcp-server :8000/mcp    │
26:                                              └───────────────────────────────┘
27:                                                              ▲
28:                                                              │ OpenAI-compatible
29:                                              ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
30:                                              │  Your local LLM backend       │
31:                                              └───────────────────────────────┘
32: ```
33: 
34: ## Interface
35: 
36: The Studio opens as a conversation, not a dashboard.
37: 
38: | Surface | What it does |
39: |---|---|
40: | **Hero** | One rotating headline above the composer: a greeting (time of day, plus your name if you set one in Settings), what is already on the canvas, or what the studio can do. It cycles every few seconds and stays still under `prefers-reduced-motion`. |
41: | **Suggestion pills** | Below the headline. Some open a workspace panel (landscape, simulate, capture), others start a conversation. They change as the canvas fills up. |
42: | **Composer** | Docked at the bottom of the transcript. `Enter` sends, `Shift`+`Enter` adds a line, `Cmd/Ctrl`+`K` focuses it, and the send button becomes a stop button while a reply streams. |
43: | **Drawer** (left) | New conversation, the five workspace panels, live model/MCP status, and Settings. Collapses to an icon rail with `Cmd/Ctrl`+`B`; becomes an overlay sheet on narrow screens. |
44: | **Workspace panel** (right) | The classic UI — opportunity landscape, job map, impact simulation, evidence, direct capture, settings — opens beside the conversation, never on top of it. |
45: 
46: Replies render Markdown (headings, lists, emphasis, inline and fenced code).
47: Tool calls appear inline as small trace chips while the agent works.
48: 
49: ## 1. Web — production build (recommended for a quick look)
50: 
51: ```bash
52: npm --prefix apps/studio run build   # build the SPA into apps/studio/dist
53: python scripts/dev.py            # starts MCP :8000 + sidecar :8100
54: ```
55: 
56: | Service | URL |
57: |---|---|
58: | MCP Server | http://localhost:8000/mcp |
59: | Living Studio | http://127.0.0.1:8100 |
60: 
61: `python scripts/dev.py` starts both processes concurrently; press **Ctrl+C** to
62: stop both.
63: 
64: ## 2. Web — dev with hot reload
65: 
66: Vite proxies `/api` to the sidecar:
67: 
68: ```bash
69: npm --prefix apps/studio run dev:full   # MCP + sidecar + Vite together
70: # open http://localhost:5173
71: ```
72: 
73: ## 3. Desktop — Tauri 2
74: 
75: The app spawns the MCP server and sidecar itself:
76: 
77: ```bash
78: npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri dev     # dev window
79: npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri build   # bundles: .deb / .AppImage (Linux), .app / .dmg (macOS), .msi / .exe (Windows)
80: ```
81: 
82: > [!NOTE]
83: > **Tauri prerequisites.** The desktop build needs the WebKitGTK toolchain and
84: > Rust 1.90+. On Debian/Ubuntu:
85: >
86: > ```bash
87: > sudo apt-get install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev build-essential pkg-config curl wget file \
88: >   libxdo-dev libssl-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf xdg-utils libfuse2t64
89: > ```
90: >
91: > The Tauri CLI ships as the `@tauri-apps/cli` npm dev dependency
92: > (`npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri`). The sidecar is launched with
93: > `uv run python -m …` from the repository root; if the app cannot locate the
94: > repo root, set `AGENTIC_ODI_REPO_ROOT`.
95: 
96: ## Desktop signing & updater secrets
97: 
98: Self-updating and code signing are **env-driven**: if a secret is absent, an
99: unsigned artifact is produced instead of failing. CI reads these from GitHub
100: Actions secrets.
101: 
102: | Secret | Purpose |
103: |---|---|
104: | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY` | Signs updater artifacts (`.sig`) and the `latest.json` manifest. A tagged release fails loudly without it. Generate with `npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri signer generate`. |
105: | `TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD` | Password for the private key (optional when the key has none). |
106: | `APPLE_CERTIFICATE` / `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | macOS Developer ID certificate (base64 `.p12`) and its password. |
107: | `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` | macOS signing identity. |
108: | `APPLE_ID` / `APPLE_PASSWORD` / `APPLE_TEAM_ID` | macOS notarization credentials. |
109: | `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE` / `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD` | Windows Authenticode PFX (base64) and its password; imported by CI and injected into the bundle config. |
110: 
111: Releases are published by `.github/workflows/tauri-release.yml` when a `v*` tag
112: is pushed. The desktop app checks for updates on startup and via
113: **Settings → Check for updates**.
114: 
115: ### Managing the updater signing key
116: 
117: The updater key pair authenticates release artifacts so an installed app can
118: verify that an auto-update genuinely came from you. The **public** key is
119: embedded in `apps/studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json` (`plugins.updater.pubkey`) and is
120: safe to commit. The **private** key must never be committed, logged, printed in
121: CI, or attached to a build artifact.
122: 
123: 1. **Generate a key pair** (only if you need a new one). Leave `-p ""` for a
124:    passwordless key, or pass a password and remember it:
125: 
126:    ```bash
127:    npm --prefix apps/studio run tauri signer generate -- -w ./living-studio.key -p "" -f
128:    ```
129: 
130:    This writes `living-studio.key` (private, `0600`) and `living-studio.key.pub`
131:    (public).
132: 
133: 2. **Paste the public key** into `apps/studio/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`:
134: 
135:    ```jsonc
136:    {
137:      "plugins": {
138:        "updater": {
139:          "endpoints": ["https://github.com/alehar9320/agentic-odi/releases/latest/download/latest.json"],
140:          "pubkey": "<contents of living-studio.key.pub>"
141:        }
142:      }
143:    }
144:    ```
145: 
146: 3. **Store the private key outside the repository** (the repo root is
147:    git-tracked; a sibling directory is not), with restricted permissions:
148: 
149:    ```bash
150:    mkdir -p ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys && chmod 700 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys
151:    mv living-studio.key ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/
152:    chmod 600 ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key
153:    ```
154: 
155:    Move it to a long-term secret store (password manager, 1Password/Bitwarden/
156:    Vault, or a private encrypted backup) when you decide where that lives.
157:    Losing it means future releases can no longer be signed for existing
158:    installs.
159: 
160: 4. **Add the private key as a GitHub Actions secret** (Settings → Secrets and
161:    variables → Actions → New repository secret), or via the CLI:
162: 
163:    ```bash
164:    gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY < ~/repos/agentic-odi-keys/living-studio.key
165:    gh secret set TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD --body ""   # only if you set a password
166:    ```
167: 
168: 5. **Verify** the secrets exist (values are never displayed):
169: 
170:    ```bash
171:    gh secret list
172:    ```
173: 
174: 6. **Rotate** by repeating steps 1–4, then publishing a release signed with the
175:    new key. Existing installs still verify against the public key compiled into
176:    their binary, so keep the old private key usable and publish the new public
177:    key ahead of the cut-over.
178: 
179: > [!CAUTION]
180: > If the private key leaks, treat auto-updates as compromised: generate a new
181: > pair, rotate the Actions secret, and publish a freshly signed release.
182: 
183: > [!IMPORTANT]
184: > **Migration note.** The Streamlit UI has been removed. The Living Studio now
185: > lives in `apps/studio/` (browser SPA + Tauri desktop app) and is served by the
186: > `apps/studio-api` sidecar on port **8100** (previously Streamlit's `8501`).
187: > Start everything with `python scripts/dev.py`. All `AGENTIC_ODI_*` environment
188: > variable names, the demo dataset, and the ODI formulas are unchanged.
189: 
190: ## Connecting an LLM
191: 
192: The Studio needs an OpenAI-compatible LLM backend with tool-calling support to
193: drive the agent. For a fully local setup, see
194: [Local LLM Backend](local-llm.md).
195: 
196: ## Agent-Driven Testing
197: 
198: Type `/dev` in the AI assistant to trigger the full automated workflow: it starts
199: both processes, opens the browser, sends a test message, and reports the results.
200: 
201: Type `/test` to have the agent run all tests and report the results
202: automatically.

(End of file - total 202 lines)
</content>

content.text:
**The Steve Jobs version**

Open it and work. There is no database choice, no setup wizard, no “connect your cloud.” The app opens on your machine, with your data, offline and private. When you want it on your other laptop or to work with a teammate, you press one thing: **“Keep my work in sync.”** You sign in; the work you already did comes with you. On the second device, you sign in and it is simply there. A teammate gets a workspace invitation, not an export file. “On this device only” remains a first-class promise, not a degraded mode. And **Export everything** is always available, because trust requires a door.

**What that implies technically**

- **The deployment chooses the store, never the user.** Local app → SQLite. Hosted app → D1. Same product behavior.
- **D1 should not be the local default.** It becomes the cloud provider when the app is hosted, or when a local user explicitly turns on sync. Privacy-first users never touch it.
- **Put the seam at the event log, not the ORM.** Your append-only `IntentStore` is already the right sync primitive. Local SQLite and D1 should store the same event rows: `event_id`, `workspace_id`, `device_id`, `server_seq`, payload. That gives offline writes, idempotent replay, cross-device restore, and team sync without duplicating `ODIService` logic.
- **Keep one domain brain.** A new `packages/cloud` provides `D1EventStore` and the sync client; `packages/core` gets an `EventStore` protocol and workspace-scoped repositories. SQLite stays the local implementation. No TypeScript rewrite of ODI logic.
- **Auth only where the data leaves the device.** Better Auth on D1 (email magic link/OAuth + organizations) fits consumer and team use; Cloudflare Access can be the enterprise adapter. Local mode needs no account.
- **Self-hosted enterprise is the same Worker + D1 under the customer’s Cloudflare account**, reached by configuration, not a fork.

Before I write the full design/plan, one scoping decision:

questions.question: What must this first PR prove end-to-end?

options.description: EventStore seam, sync-ready schema migration, SQLite/D1 providers, Worker + D1 schema, authenticated push/pull sync API, portable export/import, full tests and docs. No hosted Studio sign-in UI yet.

options.label: Full hosted Studio slice
options.description: Everything above plus SPA sign-in, workspace switcher, team invites, hosted sidecar deployment config, and an end-to-end browser test. Significantly larger.

options.label: Architecture only
options.description: Provider abstraction, event schema, and interface docs only. No Cloudflare D1 or auth implementation yet.

questions.question: Which auth approach should the cloud plane use?

options.label: Better Auth on D1 (Recommended)
options.description: Email magic link/OAuth, sessions, and organizations/teams. Self-hostable, avoids vendor lock-in, fits the enterprise tier later.

options.label: Cloudflare Access
options.description: Identity and team access handled at the edge. Strong enterprise fit, weaker consumer sign-up story.

options.label: Minimal magic-link auth
options.description: Small custom Worker auth with signed sessions. Least dependencies, most security surface we own.

"""
DBAPI implementation for Cloudflare D1.

Supports two connection modes:
1. REST API - for external connections using httpx (account_id, api_token, database_id)
2. Worker Binding - for use inside Cloudflare Python Workers (d1_binding)
"""

import os
from typing import Any, Dict, Iterator, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple, Union

try:
 import httpx

 HTTPX_AVAILABLE = True
except ImportError:
 HTTPX_AVAILABLE = False

...

# MARK: - Sync REST API Connection

class Connection:
 """DBAPI-compatible connection for Cloudflare D1 REST API."""

 def __init__(
 self, account_id: str, database_id: str, api_token: str, **kwargs: Any
 ) -> None:
 """Initialize D1 connection via REST API."""
 if not HTTPX_AVAILABLE:
 raise ImportError(
 "httpx is required for REST API connections. "
 "Install with: pip install httpx"
 )

 self.account_id = account_id
 self.database_id = database_id
 self.api_token = api_token

 # Build the D1 REST API URL, allowing override via kwarg or CF_D1_BASE_URL env var
 _default_base = (
 f"https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/{account_id}"
 f"/d1/database/{database_id}"
 )
 self.base_url = kwargs.get(
 "base_url", os.environ.get("CF_D1_BASE_URL", _default_base)
 )

 # HTTP client
 self.client = httpx.Client(
 headers={
 "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_token}",
 "Content-Type": "application/json",
 },
 timeout=30.0,
 )

 # Connection state
 self._closed = False

 def cursor(self) -> Cursor:
 """Create a cursor."""
 if self._closed:
 raise InterfaceError("Connection is closed")
 return Cursor(self)

 def close(self) -> None:
 """Close the connection."""
 if not self._closed:
 self.client.close()
 self._closed = True

 def commit(self) -> None:
 """Commit transaction (no-op for D1)."""
 # D1 auto-commits each query
 pass

 def rollback(self) -> None:
 """Rollback transaction (not supported by D1)."""
 # D1 doesn't support explicit transactions via REST API
 pass

 def execute(self, operation: str, parameters: Optional[Sequence] = None) -> Cursor:
 """Execute operation directly on connection (convenience method)."""
 cursor = self.cursor()
 cursor.execute(operation, parameters)
 return cursor

 def _execute_query(
 self, query: str, parameters: Optional[Sequence] = None
 ) -> Dict[str, Any]:
 """Internal method to execute SQL query via D1 REST API."""
 if self._closed:
 raise InterfaceError("Connection is closed")

 # Prepare the request payload
 payload: Dict[str, Any] = {"sql": query}
 params = _prepare_parameters(parameters)
 if params:
 payload["params"] = params

 try:
 # MARK: - Make request to D1 REST API /raw endpoint
 # Use /raw endpoint to get column names even on empty results
 response = self.client.post(f"{self.base_url}/raw", json=payload)
 response.raise_for_status()

 # Parse response
 data = response.json()

 if not data.get("success", False):
 errors = data.get("errors", [])
 if errors:
 error_msg = errors[0].get("message", "Unknown error")
 raise OperationalError(f"D1 API error: {error_msg}")
 else:
 raise OperationalError("D1 API request failed")

 # MARK: - Extract result data from /raw response format
 # /raw returns: {"result": [{"results": {"columns": [...], "rows": [...]}, "meta": {...}}]}
 result_data = data.get("result", [])
 if result_data:
 query_result = result_data[0]
 raw_results = query_result.get("results", {})
 columns = raw_results.get("columns", [])
 rows = raw_results.get("rows", [])

 # Convert rows from arrays to dicts using column names
 results = []
 for row in rows:
 results.append(dict(zip(columns, row)))

 return {
 "results": results,
 "columns": columns,
 "meta": query_result.get("meta", {}),
 "success": query_result.get("success", True),
 }
 else:
 return {"results": [], "columns": [], "meta": {}, "success": True}

 except httpx.RequestError as e:
 raise OperationalError(f"HTTP request failed: {e}")
 except httpx.HTTPStatusError as e:
 raise OperationalError(
 f"HTTP error {e.response.status_code}: {e.response.text}"
 )

 @property
 def closed(self) -> bool:
 """Check if connection is closed."""
 return self._closed

permissions:

jobs:
  e2e-linux-macos:
    if: github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' || github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success'
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - name: Resolve release tag
        id: tag
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          DISPATCH_TAG: ${{ inputs.tag }}
          RUN_BRANCH: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_branch }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          tag="${DISPATCH_TAG:-$RUN_BRANCH}"

            tag="$(gh api "repos/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/releases/latest" --jq .tag_name)"

          case "$tag" in
            v*) ;;

          esac
          echo "tag=$tag" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "Testing $tag"

          APP_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_CLIENT_ID }}
          APP_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY }}
        run: |
          if [ -n "$APP_CLIENT_ID" ] && [ -n "$APP_PRIVATE_KEY" ]; then
            echo "configured=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "configured=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            echo "::warning title=Release automation is degraded::RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_CLIENT_ID and/or RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY are missing, so release-please falls back to GITHUB_TOKEN. GitHub holds workflow runs created from GITHUB_TOKEN-authored pushes (\"This workflow requires approval from a maintainer\") and ignores the tag it creates, so this release needs a maintainer approval and ships without binaries. See 'Release automation' in README.md."
          fi

      - name: Create GitHub App token
        id: app-token
        if: steps.app-check.outputs.configured == 'true'
        uses: actions/create-github-app-token@v3
        with:
          client-id: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_CLIENT_ID }}
          private-key: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_PLEASE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          permission-contents: write
          permission-issues: write
          permission-pull-requests: write

      - name: Release Please
        id: release
        uses: googleapis/release-please-action@v4
        with:
          config-file: release-please-config.json
          manifest-file: .release-please-manifest.json
          token: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token || github.token }}

      - name: Arm auto-merge on the release PR
        id: auto-merge
        if: steps.release.outputs.prs_created == 'true'
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token || github.token }}
          PRS: ${{ steps.release.outputs.prs }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          for pr in $(echo "$PRS" | jq -r '.[].number'); do
            state="$(gh pr view "$pr" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --json state --jq .state)"
            if [ "$state" != "OPEN" ]; then
              echo "Skipping #$pr (state: $state)"
              continue
            fi
            echo "Arming auto-merge on #$pr"
            gh pr merge --auto --squash "$pr" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY"
          done

name: release

on:
  push:
    tags:
      - "v*"

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  build:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - os: linux
            runner: ubuntu-latest
            target: linux_x86_64
          - os: linux
            runner: ubuntu-24.04-arm
            target: linux_arm64
          - os: macos
            runner: macos-14
            target: macos_arm64
          - os: macos
            runner: macos-15-intel
            target: macos_x86_64
          - os: windows
            runner: windows-latest
            target: windows_x86_64
    # No container: the Node-based actions (checkout, setup-uv) need glibc >= 2.28,
    # which the manylinux2014 images (glibc 2.17) cannot provide. If a narrower
    # glibc floor is needed later, use a manylinux_2_28 image instead.
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.runner }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Setup uv
        uses: ./.github/actions/setup
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
      - name: Build
        env:
          TARGET: ${{ matrix.target }}
        run: |
          VERSION="${GITHUB_REF_NAME#v}"
          RELEASE_DATE_UTC="$(git log -1 --format=%cI)"
          export VERSION RELEASE_DATE_UTC
          bash scripts/build_binary.sh
      - name: Write checksums
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          shopt -s nullglob
          archives=(odi_*.tar.gz odi_*.zip)
          if [ "${#archives[@]}" -eq 0 ]; then
            echo "::error::No archive was produced for ${{ matrix.target }}"
            exit 1
          fi
          if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            sha256sum "${archives[@]}" > "checksums-${{ matrix.target }}.txt"
          elif command -v shasum >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            shasum -a 256 "${archives[@]}" > "checksums-${{ matrix.target }}.txt"
          else
            echo "::error::No sha256 tool available on ${{ matrix.runner }}"
            exit 1
          fi
          cat "checksums-${{ matrix.target }}.txt"
      - name: Upload checksums fragment
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: checksums-${{ matrix.target }}
          path: checksums-${{ matrix.target }}.txt
          if-no-files-found: error
      - name: Upload assets
        uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
        with:
          files: |
            odi_*.tar.gz
            odi_*.zip

  checksums:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          pattern: checksums-*
          path: fragments
          merge-multiple: true
      - name: Combine per-target checksums
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          cat fragments/checksums-*.txt | sort -k2 > checksums.txt
          test -s checksums.txt
          echo "checksums.txt"
          cat checksums.txt
      - name: Upload checksums.txt
        uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
        with:
          files: checksums.txt

  upload-installers:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Upload install scripts
        uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
        with:
          files: |
            scripts/install.sh
            scripts/install.ps1
### .github/workflows/tauri-release.yml
name: Tauri Release

on:
  push:
    tags:
      - "v*"
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      tag:
        description: "Existing release tag to attach desktop bundles to (e.g. v0.3.0)"
        required: true
        type: string

concurrency:
  group: tauri-release-${{ inputs.tag || github.ref_name }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  preflight:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - name: Require updater signing key
        env:
          SIGNING_KEY: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY }}
        run: |
          if [ -z "$SIGNING_KEY" ]; then
            echo "::error::TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY is required to publish a signed release; without it the updater artifacts would be broken."
            exit 1
          fi

  build:
    needs: [preflight]
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - platform: ubuntu-22.04
            args: ""
          - platform: macos-latest
            args: "--target aarch64-apple-darwin"
          - platform: macos-latest
            args: "--target x86_64-apple-darwin"
          - platform: windows-latest
            args: ""
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.platform }}
    timeout-minutes: 90
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Install Linux webview dependencies
        if: matrix.platform == 'ubuntu-22.04'
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev build-essential curl wget file \
            libxdo-dev libssl-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf

      - name: Setup Rust
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          targets: ${{ startsWith(matrix.platform, 'macos') && 'aarch64-apple-darwin,x86_64-apple-darwin' || '' }}

      - uses: swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          workspaces: apps/studio/src-tauri -> target

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: "lts/*"
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: apps/studio/package-lock.json

      - name: Install frontend dependencies
        run: npm ci
        working-directory: apps/studio

      - name: Import Windows signing certificate
        if: matrix.platform == 'windows-latest'
        shell: pwsh
        env:
          WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE: ${{ secrets.WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE }}
          WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          if ([string]::IsNullOrEmpty($env:WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE)) {
            Write-Output "No WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE secret — building unsigned Windows installer."
            exit 0
          }
          $bytes = [Convert]::FromBase64String($env:WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE)
          $path = Join-Path $env:RUNNER_TEMP "cert.pfx"
          [IO.File]::WriteAllBytes($path, $bytes)
          $secure = ConvertTo-SecureString -String $env:WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD -AsPlainText -Force
          $cert = Import-PfxCertificate -FilePath $path -CertStoreLocation Cert:\CurrentUser\My -Password $secure
          $config = '{"bundle":{"windows":{"certificateThumbprint":"' + $cert.Thumbprint + '"}}}'
          "TAURI_CONFIG=$config" | Out-File -FilePath $env:GITHUB_ENV -Append -Encoding utf8
          Write-Output "Imported Windows certificate $($cert.Thumbprint)"

      # The release already exists (release-please cuts it for the tag), so this
      # attaches the desktop bundles to it and publishes it — no draft is left
      # behind for a maintainer to publish by hand.
      - name: Build and attach release
        uses: tauri-apps/tauri-action@v1
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD }}
          APPLE_CERTIFICATE: ${{ secrets.APPLE_CERTIFICATE }}
          APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD }}
          APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY: ${{ secrets.APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY }}
          APPLE_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_ID }}
          APPLE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.APPLE_PASSWORD }}
          APPLE_TEAM_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_TEAM_ID }}
        with:
          projectPath: apps/studio
          tagName: ${{ inputs.tag || github.ref_name }}
          releaseName: ${{ inputs.tag || github.ref_name }}
          releaseDraft: false
          prerelease: false
          args: ${{ matrix.args }}

<skill_content name="writing-plans">
# Skill: writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Step Granularity

**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**

One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice
(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an
algorithm they do not determine.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## What a Step Contains

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  spec's exact values in them.
- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**
